newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's negotiator to resume dialogue with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru's negotiator to resume dialogue with rebels.

text.p: Peru's chief negotiator prepared on Sunday to meet with the leader of Marxist rebels holding 74 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's residence in an effort to hammer out a peaceful solution to the 26-day crisis.
The long-awaited meeting between Education Minister Domingo Palermo and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader Nestor Cerpa was expected to take place later on Sunday.
News of renewed contact between the two sides was welcomed in Tokyo, where concern remained high over the two dozen Japanese diplomats and officials still held inside the ambassador's home.
"I expect direct negotiations this time to be held smoothly and vigorously and bring about a tangible resolution," Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told the NHK television network.

While seeking an early resolution of the standoff, Ikeda reiterated Tokyo's concern that the lives of the remaining hostages remained paramount. "The most important thing is the safe release of all the hostages. This should take priority over the time element," he said.

Palermo, the government's chief negotiator in the crisis, arranged the meeting with Cerpa in a brief radio conversation witnessed by a small group of foreign correspondents on Friday. The two men have not met since a first face-to-face meeting inside the residence on Dec. 28, although they have exchanged several written messages.
The MRTA took more than 500 hostages when it stormed a cocktail party at the residence on Dec. 17, but released the majority in what it has called "goodwill gestures."

The rebels are holding on to the most valuable hostages -- including dozens of top government and security force officials and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori -- as bargaining chips to obtain their main demand, the release of about 400 jailed comrades.
Fujimori has insisted he will not give in to "terrorist blackmail" and has urged the rebels to lay down their arms and release all the captives under the supervision of a "guarantor committee."
The government has, however, floated the possibility of granting the rebels political exile abroad if they surrender.
In a further sign that talks with the rebels had been revived, Roman Catholic bishop Juan Carlos Cipriani returned to the residence on Saturday to visit the hostages.

"I am optimistic that everything will turn out well," Cipriani, whose visits to the besieged diplomatic mansion have often been associated with hostage releases, told reporters before entering the residence.
While negotiations to end the conflict appeared to be back on track, Peruvian authorities maintained a tough line against the MRTA.

"We consider it as a terrorist organisation because it causes fear, panic, chaos and destruction," Col. Alberto Sarmiento of Peru's National Police, told a news conference organised by the government public relations unit Promperu.

The only sign of life on Saturday from the roughly 15 MRTA members inside was the brief appearance at a window of one young rebel dressed in black who watched photographers on a nearby rooftop with binoculars.
When asked by the photographers how the hostages were, the rebel first replied "screwed up" and then said "fine."

Asked if there would be more hostage releases or if the rebels were still demanding that the government free all of their jailed comrades, he waved his hands in a gesture interpreted by some journalists as meaning "No."
The rebels are armed with automatic rifles and grenades and have booby-trapped and mined the diplomatic compound against a surprise attack.
Two journalists who sneaked past police for an interview with Cerpa were released by antiterrorist police on Saturday night.

Japan's TV Asahi reporter Tsuyoshi Hitomi and his Peruvian interpreter Victor Borja had been detained for four days and were strongly criticised by both Peruvian and Japanese authorities for jeopardising efforts to end the siege.

Hitomi left Peru under tight security early on Sunday on a flight to New York, where he is based. Hitomi's taped interview with Cerpa was in the hands of Japanese Foreign Ministry officials in Lima, his lawyer Augusto Linares told reporters.
